summary: Describes how the Session Description Protocol offer/answer exchange is used to carry out Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE), the method endpoints use to find a working path through NATs. It is standards-track and obsoletes RFC 5245 and RFC 6336.

eli5.summary: Before two computers can talk through a maze of home networks, they swap notes about how to reach each other. This document explains how those notes are written and exchanged so they can find a path that works.

questions: how does ice use sdp offer answer
subtitle: How two endpoints write down their possible network paths in SDP offers and answers so ICE can pick one that works.

tldr.problem: ICE finds a working media path through NATs, but it needs a way to carry each side's candidate addresses and credentials to the other. RFC 5245 once mixed the general ICE rules with the SDP-specific details.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC maps ICE onto the SDP offer/answer exchange: candidates go into candidate attributes, credentials into ice-ufrag and ice-pwd, and later offers update the chosen path or restart ICE.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5245 and RFC 6336 and leaves the common ICE procedures to RFC 8445, so SDP users read this document for the offer/answer details.

today: RFC 8839 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It obsoletes RFC 5245 and RFC 6336, and the common ICE procedures it relies on are in RFC 8445.

sections.title: What This Document Adds to ICE
sections.content:
Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) is defined in RFC 8445. That RFC covers the procedures common to every use of ICE. This document gives the extra details needed when ICE runs inside the SDP offer/answer model of RFC 3264.

Previously both parts lived in RFC 5245. When RFC 8445 replaced it, the SDP-specific details were removed, and this RFC picks them up. It obsoletes RFC 5245 and RFC 6336.

In this mapping the offerer is the ICE initiating agent and the answerer is the responding agent. The controlling and controlled roles are still decided by the rules in RFC 8445.
sections.eli5: There is a big rulebook for how computers find a path to each other. This is the small extra booklet that says how to write the notes down in the session description.

sections.title: How ICE Is Encoded in SDP
sections.content:
Each ICE data stream is one SDP media description (an m= section). Each candidate for that stream, including the default candidate, is written as an a=candidate attribute. The username fragment and password become ice-ufrag and ice-pwd.

Before a pair is nominated, the c= and m= lines carry the default candidate, which is the address a non-ICE agent would use. After nomination they carry the nominated candidate instead.

An ICE-lite implementation MUST include ice-lite; a full implementation MUST NOT. A compliant agent MUST include ice-options with the ice2 value. If a peer shows ICE support but omits ice2, the agent can assume the peer follows RFC 5245. If RTCP is not used, the agent signals that with RS:0 and RR:0. The rtcp attribute may be left out when RTCP uses the next port up on the same address.
sections.eli5: Each way to reach you is written on its own line, like listing phone numbers where someone could call you. One line also holds your secret code word so only the right caller gets through.

sections.title: The Initial Offer and Answer
sections.content:
In the initial offer, the offerer MUST include a candidate attribute for every available candidate in each m= section, plus ice-ufrag, ice-pwd and ice-options with ice2. A full implementation SHOULD add ice-pacing; a lite one MUST NOT, since it does not run connectivity checks.

An agent shows ICE support by including at least ice-pwd and ice-ufrag. The answerer follows the same rules and MUST use the same transport protocol as the offer. If it does not accept ICE, or the offer did not show ICE support, it MUST NOT put ICE attributes in the answer. Once the answer is sent, the answerer can start connectivity checks.

An offer or answer may have no candidates at all, with the default destination set to 0.0.0.0 (or ::) and port 9. That means the sender will rely on peer-reflexive candidates or send more candidates later. A fully qualified domain name as the default destination is also not an ICE failure.

If the default destination does not appear among the candidates, a responder MAY answer with ice-mismatch and fall back to plain RFC 3264 for that stream. This is optional in this RFC.
sections.eli5: You hand over your list of ways to reach you and your code word. The other side does the same. If they do not know the game, you just talk the normal way.

sections.title: Concluding ICE and Later Offers
sections.content:
When a pair is nominated for a checklist, that checklist is Completed. If the nominated pair differs from the default pair and the peer did not signal ice2, the controlling agent MUST send a new offer whose c= and m= lines match the nominated pair. With ice2 it can wait until its next offer. A Failed checklist means the controlling agent MUST send an offer that removes that stream by setting its port to zero.

After nomination, the offer lists only the nominated local candidates, one per component. A controlling agent also adds remote-candidates for each Completed stream, to avoid a race where the updated offer reaches the controlled agent before the connectivity checks do. If the answerer sees a pair that has not yet been confirmed valid, it waits for in-progress checks, or restarts ICE if the checks failed.

To restart ICE, an agent MUST change both ice-pwd and ice-ufrag. Setting the connection address to 0.0.0.0 would also trigger a restart, so ICE implementations MUST NOT use it for call hold and MUST use inactive or sendonly instead. A restart is the only time ice-options, ice-pacing and ice-lite may change. During a restart the agent keeps sending media on the previous selected pair.

Lite implementations have their own rules: they MUST NOT add host candidates or change credentials in a later offer without a restart. If two lite-controlling agents send offers at once, the signaling protocol decides the winner and the loser becomes controlled.
sections.eli5: Once you find a path that works, you tell the other side which one you picked so you both stop guessing. If something goes wrong, you can start over with a fresh code word.

sections.title: The Eight SDP Attributes
sections.content:
The grammar section defines eight new attributes in ABNF. A candidate line holds a foundation, a component ID, a transport (only UDP is defined), a priority, an address, a port and a type such as host, srflx, prflx or relay. Server-reflexive, peer-reflexive and relayed candidates MUST carry raddr and rport; host candidates MUST omit them. For privacy, a sender can use 0.0.0.0 or :: and port 9 there. Component ID 1 is RTP and 2 is RTCP. An agent MUST NOT use FQDNs in its own candidates and MUST ignore remote candidates that use them.

The ice-ufrag value has 4 to 256 characters and ice-pwd has 22 to 256, chosen randomly. The ufrag MUST NOT be longer than 32 characters when sent, but an implementation MUST accept up to 256. The ice-pacing value is the desired check interval in milliseconds, defaulting to 50 ms. When both agents state a value, both use the larger one.

Unknown name/value extensions on a candidate line MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: The notes have a fixed format, like a form with boxes for the address, the port and what kind of address it is. The code word has to be long and random so nobody can guess it.

sections.title: SIP, Keepalives and Gateways
sections.content:
ICE agents send keepalives following RFC 8445 whatever the stream direction. With SIP, ICE is not meant for NAT traversal of the SIP signaling itself. When a call forks, ICE runs separately for each answer, and the username fragments in connectivity checks also let the caller tell which callee a media stream comes from.

To cut delay, the caller is RECOMMENDED to gather candidates before sending the INVITE. An answerer SHOULD hold off alerting the user until candidates have entered the valid list, which avoids "ghost rings" where the callee picks up and hears nothing. If an ICE-lite peer is retransmitting a provisional response, it MUST stop after sending it four times.

Application Layer Gateways (ALGs) that rewrite SDP can break ICE. ICE does not try to work around broken ALGs, but the ice-mismatch attribute helps diagnose them. Running signaling over TLS prevents the ALG from changing the SDP, and implementations behind ALGs SHOULD support TLS for SDP.
sections.eli5: If a helper in the middle scribbles on your notes, the plan can break. Sealing the notes in an envelope, which is what TLS does, stops that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general security considerations of RFC 8445 and RFC 3264 apply. An attacker who can modify offers and answers could redirect media to a DoS target or insert themselves into the stream, so the RFC says TLS is RECOMMENDED for signaling.

The voice hammer attack is an amplification attack in which a participant puts a victim's address in the SDP as the media destination. With ICE, the receiver first runs connectivity checks to that address, and a third-party host will not answer them, so no media is sent. This only helps when ICE is actually used. A SIP UA that refuses non-ICE answers MUST include an ice option tag in its Require header.
sections.eli5: Before sending a big pile of video to an address, ICE knocks and waits for an answer. If nobody there answers, nothing is sent, so a trickster cannot aim your video at an innocent house.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 5245
sections.content:
This document lists the SDP-specific changes from RFC 5245. The common changes, such as dropping aggressive nomination, are described in RFC 8445.

  • The ice2 option and the ice-pacing attribute are defined.
  • Agents must not generate candidates with FQDNs and must discard such candidates from a peer.
  • The rtcp attribute is no longer always required.
  • ICE mismatch is now optional, and default candidates that are FQDNs or 0.0.0.0/:: with port 9 do not trigger it.

The IANA section registers the eight attributes, keeps the ICE Options registry and creates a Candidate Attribute Extensions subregistry.
sections.eli5: This is the list of what changed since the old rulebook, like patch notes for a game.
